description: AerO-Club is an engineering club at AIAC dedicated to aviation, electronics, and technological innovation. It brings together passionate students to collaborate on technical projects, explore new technologies, develop practical skills, and turn creative ideas into real-world solutions through teamwork and innovation.
summary:
DOORAtmosphere is an interactive website that opens a “door” to Earth’s atmosphere. It turns raw NASA data into clear, tested answers about how nine variables changed between 2004 and 2026: aerosols (AOT), methane, water vapour, ozone, NO₂, solar irradiation, wind, snowmelt and vegetation (NDVI).

We downloaded NetCDF files from NASA Giovanni, GES DISC and Earthdata (MERRA-2, Aura OMI, Aura MLS, MODIS). We cleaned them in Python on Google Colab, keeping missing values missing and never inventing data, and aggregated them into semesters. Each series then goes through two independent trend tests (regression with autocorrelation correction and Mann-Kendall with the Sen slope) before a verdict is given. The website, built in VS Code with Plotly, lets anyone act as a Trend Detective. You pick a variable, a period and a region, and get a verdict with its limits. You can also compare Morocco with the world and explore maps, figures and a 3D globe.

The project matters because scattered datasets and noisy signals make atmospheric change hard to judge. We bring the whole data journey into one open, reproducible place, from raw file to verdict. Scientists, students, Moroccan decision-makers and curious citizens can use it without writing code.
details:
What it does and how it works

DOORAtmosphere is a web platform that lets anyone investigate how Earth's atmosphere has changed from 2004 to 2026, from the whole planet down to Morocco. It covers nine variables:

  • Aerosol optical thickness (AOT)
  • Methane (CH₄)
  • Water vapour (H₂O, 30 pressure levels)
  • Ozone (O₃)
  • Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)
  • Surface solar irradiation (SW)
  • Wind speed at 50 m
  • Snowmelt
  • Vegetation (NDVI)

Our pipeline has five steps:

  1. Download. We download NetCDF (.nc) files from NASA Giovanni, GES DISC and Earthdata.
    • inspection
    • name standardisation
    • NASA fill values set to NaN
    • duplicates removed
    • physical-range checks
    • date conversion
    • outliers flagged but never deleted automatically
    • gap checks
    • validation and export
    • a least-squares regression corrected for autocorrelation
    • a Mann-Kendall test (Hamed–Rao) with the Sen slope
  2. Publish. The results are shown on the website.

The site has eight sections:

  • Home: a 3D globe with the Aura/OMI satellite in orbit.
  • Earth Explorer: maps.
  • Variables: one fact sheet per variable, with figures and plain-language explanations.
  • Trend Detective: choose a variable, a start and end semester and regions, then run the tests.
  • Morocco: values at major cities and an analysis of every variable over the country.
  • Global Comparison: Morocco vs World, with a statistical test of the difference.
  • Methodology: every step and its limits.
  • About: the team and a summary of every dataset.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Scientists and students get cleaned semester series, tested trends and open, reproducible code.
  • Moroccan decision-makers get local evidence for air quality, solar and wind energy, agriculture and water planning.
  • Curious citizens can explore 22 years of NASA observations without writing code.

Our goal is to make atmospheric detection approachable and to make people want to learn more about it. Adding a new variable only needs one clean CSV and one script run, so the platform can grow.

Tools and technologies

  • Analysis: Python on Google Colab, with xarray, pandas, NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib.
    • MERRA-2 (AOT, irradiation, wind)
    • Aura OMI (ozone, NO₂)
    • Aura MLS (water vapour)
    • Terra MODIS MOD13C2 (NDVI)
    • NASA Giovanni (methane, snowmelt)

No special hardware was used.

Creativity

The name DOORAtmosphere is a playful nod to Dora the Explorer, a curious explorer who investigates, just as our "Trend Detective" does and as the OMI instrument does from orbit. It is also a "door" into the atmosphere's chemical and physical variables. The website presents the analysis as an investigation in eight steps: discover, select, explore, visualise, analyse, compare, interpret, reveal. It uses animations, a live 3D globe and a day/night theme.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty. We never fill or invent data. Every variable shows its source and its type (satellite observation, reanalysis or team figure), and every verdict shows its limits and its confidence interval.
  • Statistical robustness. Two independent tests must agree, autocorrelation is corrected, and a minimum record length is required.
  • Seasonality. We use semester analysis, with anomalies computed for each semester type.
  • Area-weighted averages. Spatial means are weighted by the cosine of latitude.
  • A local focus on Morocco, compared against the world.
  • Accessibility. Simple language, few icons, a mobile-friendly layout, and pages that load offline.

Team

AerO-Club, from AEROLEC, the robotics, electrical and electronics club of the Académie Internationale Mohammed VI de l'Aviation Civile (AIAC). We are six engineering students in Electrical, Electronic & Telecom engineering and IT: Aya LACHKAR, Abderazzak ASMAY, Naouar EL KENDI, Said OUKAAI, Asmae EL GHAZI and Omar BENRAQQOUCH.
